The bell above the door had been broken since spring, so Mira learned to know the customers by their footsteps: the slow scuff of the newspaper man, the twins who arrived at a run and left at a run. She had worked the register at her grandmother's shop every Saturday since March, and had come to think of the drawer as hers — the worn ridge in the coin tray, the rubber band she kept around the twenties.

On the last Saturday in October she forgot her jacket and went back for it after closing. Through the window she saw her grandmother at the counter with the drawer open, counting. Mira stood in the cold and watched her finger travel down the column of the receipt tape, stop, and go back up. Then her grandmother took a small purse from her coat pocket, counted out four bills, and laid them in the drawer.

Mira did not go in. She walked to the bus stop with her jacket over her arm and the word for it arriving near the corner: checked. She was being checked. Every Saturday since March. All that talk about trusting her with the shop, and a woman in an empty room counting after her.

She said nothing for a week. Then, on a Tuesday, flattening boxes for the recycling, she found the tapes in a bundle and read them the way her grandmother had, down the column. The totals were short. Not by much — three dollars, eleven, six. On the days she had worked the register alone, they were short. On the days her grandmother had worked it, they were not.

She sat down on the step with the tapes in her lap. Her grandmother had not been counting to catch her. She had been counting to find out how much, and paying it in from her own purse, so the books would balance and Mira would never be told. A whole spring and summer of it. Mira thought about the rubber band around the twenties, how carefully she had put it there, and how little that had ever had to do with anything.

Ravi went to the address with sixty dollars folded in his pocket and a list of things to point out: the rust at the chainstay, the frayed brake cable, the tires that would have to be replaced before anyone rode it anywhere. The advertisement had said one hundred, or best offer.

The man who wheeled the bicycle out of the garage was old enough that the walk down the drive took a while. He stood it upright between them and said nothing at all, which Ravi had not planned for. So Ravi began: the rust, the cable, the tires. The man listened with his hands behind his back and agreed with every item. Yes. Yes, that would want doing. Yes, those are perished.

"Sixty," Ravi said.

"All right."

It came so fast that Ravi heard himself say "Sixty-five" before he could stop it, and the man smiled for the first time and took the sixty-five. Then he asked one question — "You'll ride it, though?" — and Ravi said yes, of course, and wheeled it away down the drive with the particular lightness of having done well.

He spent the evening with it in the garage. Under the saddle, where four decades of weather had never reached, there was a strip of deep blue the rest of the frame had lost, and lettering: a name, and beneath the name a number, 47, the size riders pin to their backs. He turned the bicycle over and found the number again, stamped into the metal at the base of the frame. The tires were perished because nothing had been asked of them in years. Nothing else on the machine was worn at all.

Ravi sat back on his heels. He went over the conversation in the drive and could not find one moment where the man had tried for more money. He had agreed to every fault. He had asked for one thing, and Ravi had answered it on his way to the gate, without hearing it, in a hurry to get home and tell everyone the price.

The man who wheeled the bicycle out of the garage was old enough that the walk down the drive took a while. He stood it upright between them and said nothing at all, which Ravi had not planned for. So Ravi began: the rust, the cable, the tires. The man listened with his hands behind his back and agreed with every item. Yes. Yes, that would want doing. Yes, those are perished.

"Sixty," Ravi said.

"All right."

It came so fast that Ravi heard himself say "Sixty-five" before he could stop it, and the man smiled for the first time and took the sixty-five. Then he asked one question — "You'll ride it, though?" — and Ravi said yes, of course, and wheeled it away down the drive with the particular lightness of having done well.

He spent the evening with it in the garage. Under the saddle, where four decades of weather had never reached, there was a strip of deep blue the rest of the frame had lost, and lettering: a name, and beneath the name a number, 47, the size riders pin to their backs. He turned the bicycle over and found the number again, stamped into the metal at the base of the frame. The tires were perished because nothing had been asked of them in years. Nothing else on the machine was worn at all.

Ravi sat back on his heels. He went over the conversation in the drive and could not find one moment where the man had tried for more money. He had agreed to every fault. He had asked for one thing, and Ravi had answered it on his way to the gate, without hearing it, in a hurry to get home and tell everyone the price.

Hannah had told the story about the ladder so often that she had stopped noticing she was telling it. She was six; a kite had gone onto the garage roof; she had put the ladder up herself and climbed it and then would not come down, not for an hour, while her mother stood at the bottom and never raised her voice. It was the story she offered whenever anyone asked what she had been like as a child. It meant: I was not always careful.

They were clearing the house that August, and she told it again over a box of curtains, to nobody in particular. Beatriz went on folding.

"That was me," Beatriz said.

Hannah's objection did not carry. Her sister was not arguing. Without looking up she supplied the things Hannah did not have — that the kite was green, that the ladder had been borrowed from the people next door and had to go back before dark, that Hannah had been two years old and asleep indoors through the whole of it. She gave these the way you give someone directions to a street you use every day. It was plain that she had not thought about the afternoon in years, and plain that she did not understand what it was costing to hear.

Hannah went out to the garage. The gutter had come away at one end. She stood on the concrete and looked up at the edge of the roof, and then she understood something that had nothing to do with kites. She had always seen that roof from exactly here — from below, from the ground, the ladder going up and away from her. In all the years of telling it she had never once pictured the yard as it would look from up there.

She had been remembering the kitchen table. Her mother's voice, the bit where everyone laughed.

She waited to feel robbed, and did not, quite. What she felt was closer to curiosity: she had carried one piece of evidence about herself for ten years, and now she would have to find out what she was like without it.

The class met on Thursdays in a room that smelled of turpentine, and by the third week Samir had worked out how to be good at it.

The trick was scale. Draw a hand the size of a coin and nobody can see that you do not know how a thumb joins a palm. Draw the pier from far enough back and each boat becomes three confident marks. He filled a page a week that way, and the pages were admired; people leaned over them on their way past to the sink.

What he could not explain was Ms. Arno. She would look at his page for as long as politeness required, say something true and small — good weight in the water, that sky works — and then go and sit for twenty minutes beside Ilse Brandt, whose drawings were terrible. Everybody knew they were terrible. Ilse drew the same chair every week, always too large for the paper, one leg fighting the others, and every week she started it again.

In the ninth week Ilse was out sick and her book was left on the sill, and Samir, waiting for a wash to dry, turned it over.

There were fifty chairs in it. Not fifty drawings — fifty attempts at one chair, and they were not the same. In the early ones the legs went wrong. Then the legs came right and the seat floated above them. Then the seat sat down and the back was flat, and forty pages in, something in the back had begun to turn away from him into the room.

He put the book down and got out his own. Forty-odd pages: a hand, a pier, a dog, a window, a jug. Each thing once. Not one of them wrong.

He stood at the sill a while. Then he took a fresh sheet and drew the chair by the door, life-size, and it came out badly, and he understood that Ms. Arno would have nothing at all to say about it, and that this was the first honest hour he had spent in that room.

I lost a great deal. What I did afterward was reliable: I shook hands, I said "nice game" and meant it, I put the pieces back in the box in their two neat rows, and I went and got a drink from the machine in the corridor. I was good at it, too. I could hear a sentence in one language and have it out in the other before the person behind the counter had finished being impatient. I was praised for this, by her and by them — what a help he is — and I took the praise seriously, the way you take a wage.

Asked how the pain was, my mother would answer at length. I would listen to all of that and say: "Since March. Worse on stairs." I thought I was being efficient, and I was being efficient. I was also deciding, at eleven years old, which parts of my mother were relevant.

The doctor met a brisk woman who gave short answers and never wandered. There is no such woman. I built her over four or five years of appointments, and the better I built her the more smoothly they ran, and the more everyone thanked me.

I still do some of this, on the telephone, when I am tired. But I have learned to leave the sister in. The summer I was sixteen I was paid to put books back in the right place, which I took, at the start, to be the whole of the job.

The library gave me a cart and a rule. Novels by author; everything else by a number, and within a number by author again. I was fast. I could clear a cart in forty minutes, and I liked the moment at the end of a shelf when the numbers ran up without a gap — the whole row agreeing with itself.

What irritated me was the back room, where the books that had strayed came in. Somebody had filed the bee-keeping book under gardening. Somebody had left three books about one shipwreck on the table by the window, though they belonged in three separate places: one with history, one with ships, one among the local pamphlets. I put them back. Every Thursday for two months I put them back.

In August a man came to the desk and asked for "the shipwreck books — the ones that were by the window." Not a title. Not a number. The window.

I fetched them for him, one from each of three floors, and carrying them down I understood that somebody had built that pile on purpose, that it had cost them an afternoon, and that I had taken it apart every week in the belief that I was tidying.

The catalogue describes a library in which each book has one place and stays in it. Nobody reads that library. What people actually want comes in threes and fours and does not match: a pile by a window is an argument somebody is putting together, and it survives exactly as long as no one efficient walks past.

I still think the numbers should be right. I would file the bee-keeping book under bees tomorrow. But I no longer assume that a book out of place is a mistake, and when I come across three of them sitting together now, I look at them before I pick them up.
